metadata.title: Regional drinks and drinking rituals
metadata.method: Hand-compiled cultural guide, not a consumption survey. One useful headline per NUTS 2 region; the popup carries the local exceptions.
sources: Official national and regional tourism boards for Spain and Portugal
Protected geographical indication and denomination bodies where applicable

regions.ritual: White wine with seafood; licor café or orujo comes after the meal.
regions.also: Mencía reds, Estrella Galicia beer.
regions.note: Galicia is wine-and-seafood country first; the coffee liqueur is the emphatic full stop.

regions.ritual: Buy a bottle, not a glass; it is poured high in small culines and drunk at once.
regions.also: Weekend vermouth, often before lunch.
regions.note: The cider ritual is the regional identity. Vermouth is real too, but it is the aperitif rather than the headline.

regions.ritual: A small digestif after a mountain lunch; crema de orujo is the gentler version.
regions.also: Caña and vermouth with rabas around Santander.
regions.note: Coastal aperitivo culture and inland distilling coexist in a very small region.

regions.drink: Txakoli — or a marianito in Bilbao
regions.ritual: With pintxos, order txakoli, a zurito, or ask specifically for a marianito preparado.
regions.also: Sagardoa cider in a cider house; Rioja Alavesa wine inland.
regions.note: A plain marianito can mean a small vermouth. Bilbao's preparado is the cocktail: vermouth sharpened with gin, bitters and usually Campari.

regions.ritual: Sloe liqueur served cold after lunch or dinner.
regions.also: Navarra rosado and vermouth before lunch.
regions.note: Pacharán is the digestif; the everyday aperitif is more likely wine, beer or vermouth.

regions.ritual: A glass with food; in fiestas look for zurracapote, wine macerated with fruit and spice.
regions.also: Vermouth and a short caña.
regions.note: The famous export is also the ordinary local drink.

regions.ritual: A glass with tapas or roast meat; old-vine Campo de Borja and Calatayud are the signatures.
regions.also: Vermouth in Zaragoza; Ambar beer.
regions.note: Aragón's useful answer is a grape rather than one denomination.

regions.ritual: On tap before lunch, with an olive and something salty; a caña is the parallel order.
regions.also: Chinchón anisette after a long meal.
regions.note: Madrid absorbs every Spanish drinking habit, but the vermouth hour is its most legible one.

regions.drink: Ribera, Rueda or a local clarete
regions.ritual: Order a chato — a small tumbler of wine — with tapas.
regions.also: Cider in the north-west; orujo after mountain meals.
regions.note: A huge region cannot honestly be reduced to one bottle: red in Ribera, white in Rueda, clarete around Cigales and León.

regions.ritual: Young wine with food; ask what is local rather than defaulting to a famous label from elsewhere.
regions.also: Resolí, the spiced coffee-and-anise liqueur of Cuenca.
regions.note: This is the world's great broad plain of vines; the smaller ritual is Cuenca's digestif.

regions.ritual: Rustic, small-production wine in a bar or village meal; it may arrive in an unlabelled jug.
regions.also: Ribera del Guadiana wine and local fruit liqueurs.
regions.note: Pitarra describes a tradition more than a polished regional style.

regions.ritual: Midday vermut with olives, crisps and conserves; cava belongs to celebrations and long lunches.
regions.also: Cava, ratafia and a caña.
regions.note: Barcelona made the vermouth hour fashionable again; Reus never needed the reminder.

regions.ritual: After an esmorzaret: coffee burned with rum, sugar, citrus and spices.
regions.also: Agua de València as a shared evening pitcher; horchata without alcohol.
regions.note: Agua de València is the famous city cocktail. Cremaet is the more revealing everyday ritual beyond the postcard.

regions.ritual: Mallorca: palo as aperitif or herbes after food. Menorca: gin with cloudy lemonade becomes pomada.
regions.also: Herbes Eivissenques in Ibiza; local wine on every island.
regions.note: There is no honest Balearic-wide single drink: each island keeps its own bottle.

regions.ritual: Very cold and with food; rebujito — fino or manzanilla with lemon-lime soda — belongs to ferias.
regions.also: Sweet Málaga wine in the east; oloroso and amontillado around Jerez.
regions.note: The sherry family rules the west. Eastern Andalucía has its own Málaga and Granada traditions.

regions.ritual: In Cartagena: espresso layered with condensed milk, brandy and Licor 43, often with cinnamon and lemon peel.
regions.also: Local Monastrell wine and Estrella de Levante beer.
regions.note: It looks like coffee and behaves like a digestif.

regions.ritual: A sweet glass in a café, reflecting Ceuta's Spanish, Moroccan and Jewish currents.
regions.also: Beer, wine and coffee depending on the neighbourhood.
regions.note: The useful cultural marker is tea, not an invented single alcoholic identity.

regions.ritual: Sweet tea or coffee in the café culture shared across the strait.
regions.also: Beer and Spanish wine are easy to find.
regions.note: Melilla's drinking culture is mixed; tea best explains what makes it different from the mainland.

regions.ritual: Layered coffee with condensed milk, Licor 43, cinnamon and citrus; order it after food.
regions.also: Ron miel, Malvasía wine; on other islands ask for the local variation.
regions.note: The coffee is Tenerife-led, not pan-island law. Canarian rum and volcanic wine travel better across the archipelago.

regions.drink: Vinho Verde — with Port waiting after
regions.ritual: Crisp young wine with food; in Porto, finish with a small glass of Port rather than starting there.
regions.also: Super Bock as the everyday northern beer.
regions.note: Vinho Verde belongs to the wider north; Port belongs to the Douro and the city built around its trade.

regions.ritual: A strawberry-tree fruit spirit after food; amarguinha is the softer almond alternative, often with lemon and ice.
regions.also: Algarve wine and a cold imperial beer.
regions.note: Medronho is the inland, homemade-tasting answer to the resort coast.

regions.ritual: Dry sparkling wine with leitão; the bubbles and acidity are there to cut through the roast.
regions.also: Dão reds and whites, cherry liqueur around Fundão.
regions.note: Centro is several wine countries; Bairrada supplies the most distinctive table ritual.

regions.ritual: A tiny standing drink in Lisbon; answer com elas or sem elas — with or without the cherries.
regions.also: An imperial of beer; Carcavelos wine west of the city.
regions.note: A shot-sized ritual rather than an evening cocktail.

regions.ritual: A small aromatic glass after a meal, often with dessert or cheese.
regions.also: Palmela wine and a cold beer by the fish restaurants.
regions.note: The peninsula's unmistakable bottle is fortified muscat.

regions.ritual: Wine fermented in great clay amphorae; November cellar openings are the ceremonial moment.
regions.also: Alentejo reds and whites; medronho nearer the Algarve border.
regions.note: The talha is an ancient method still treated as a social event, not a museum piece.

regions.ritual: A small cherry liqueur, often served in an edible chocolate cup in Óbidos.
regions.also: Lighter Lisboa-region wines and beer on the coast.
regions.note: A town-specific ritual is used here because the statistical region itself is new and culturally broad.

regions.ritual: A chilled local fruit liqueur after food; Pico's fortified Lajido also appears in modern tonics.
regions.also: Especial beer, Pico wine and tea from São Miguel.
regions.note: Nine islands means nine answers; fruit liqueurs are the common shorthand, not the whole story.

regions.ritual: Cane spirit, honey and citrus mixed fresh; drink it with a small dentinho snack and respect its strength.
regions.also: Madeira wine and Coral beer.
regions.note: The fisherman's lemon version is the classic; passion fruit and tangerine are now everywhere.
